title: Listening practice: Kinds of Books, a Bakery Problem, and a Bridge Story
description: Three clips to listen to twice: a librarian talk, a student explaining a math solution, and a narrated story from a local museum.

stimuli.title: Listen: A visit from the librarian

turns.speaker: Librarian
turns.text: Hello, readers! Today I want to tell you about three kinds of books in our library. Fiction books tell made-up stories, like adventures and mysteries. Nonfiction books give true facts about real things, like animals, space, or people from history. Poetry books are full of poems, and poems often use rhyme and short lines. In our library, fiction books have letters on the label, and nonfiction books have numbers. If you cannot find a book, please ask me!

stimuli.script: Librarian: Hello, readers! Today I want to tell you about three kinds of books in our library. Fiction books tell made-up stories, like adventures and mysteries. In our library, fiction books have letters on the label, and nonfiction books have numbers. If you cannot find a book, please ask me!

stimuli.title: Listen: Solving a bakery problem

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: Hi, everyone. I will explain how I solved our bakery problem. A bakery makes six trays of muffins, and each tray holds eight muffins. In the morning, the bakery sells fourteen muffins. How many are left? First, I needed to find how many muffins the bakery made, so I multiplied: six times eight is forty-eight. Next, I subtracted the muffins that were sold: forty-eight minus fourteen is thirty-four. So thirty-four muffins are left. To check, I added: thirty-four plus fourteen is forty-eight.

stimuli.title: Listen: A story from Marlow Creek

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Welcome to the Marlow Creek Museum. Let me tell you how our town got its first bridge. In the spring of eighteen ninety, heavy rain made the creek rise, and the only wooden crossing washed away. For weeks, children could not get to school, and farmers could not carry their vegetables to the market. So the neighbors held a meeting. They decided that everyone would help. Some families gave wood, and others gave money. In the fall, the town finished a strong stone bridge. On opening day, the children crossed first, and the farmers followed with their carts. Today, that stone bridge is still the oldest bridge in town.

items.stem: What is the librarian mostly talking about?

options.text: Different kinds of books in the library
How to write a poem with rhyme and short lines
Where to find books about space and animals
How to ask the librarian for help at the desk

distractors.b: Poetry is one of the three kinds. The whole talk is about more than poems.
distractors.c: Space is one example of nonfiction. It is only a small detail.
distractors.d: Asking for help is the last sentence, not the main topic.

items.explanation: The librarian says she will tell about three kinds of books in the library, and then describes fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.

support.clue: Listen to the first two sentences and to the last sentence. Ask what the whole talk is about, not one small detail.
support.frame: The librarian is mostly talking about ______.
support.model: Mentor example. A chef says: 'Today we have soups, salads, and breads.' Then the chef describes each one. The chef is mostly talking about the kinds of food on the menu. Decide what the librarian's whole talk is about.

misconceptions.b: takes one detail as the main idea
misconceptions.c: takes one detail as the main idea
misconceptions.d: takes the last sentence as the main idea

items.stem: Match each kind of book to what the librarian says about it.

right.text: Often uses rhyme and short lines

items.explanation: Fiction books have letters on the label, nonfiction books have numbers, and poems often use rhyme and short lines.

support.clue: Listen for the three kinds of books. The librarian says more about each kind right after naming it.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Apples are sweet and crunchy. Lemons are sour. Bananas are soft.' Each fruit is followed by its description. Match each kind of book to its description in the same way.

facts: Fiction is made-up writing; nonfiction gives true information about real things; poems often use rhyme and short lines.
The label rule (letters on fiction, numbers on nonfiction) belongs to the invented library in this practice item.

items.stem: Which two things does the librarian say about fiction books?

options.text: They tell made-up stories.
They give true facts.
They have letters on the label.
They have numbers on the label.

distractors.b: The librarian says nonfiction books give true facts.
distractors.d: The librarian says nonfiction books have numbers on the label.

items.explanation: The librarian says fiction books tell made-up stories and have letters on the label.

support.clue: Listen for the word 'fiction'. The librarian says two things about fiction books.
support.frame: Fiction books ______, and they have ______ on the label.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Sneakers are comfortable, and they have laces.' Two true details about one thing can be joined with 'and'. Choose the two details that belong to fiction books.

facts: The label rule (letters on fiction, numbers on nonfiction) belongs to the invented library in this practice item.

items.stem: Why did Dara multiply six times eight?

options.text: To find how many muffins were sold
To find how many muffins were left
To find how many muffins were made
To check her answer in a different way

distractors.a: Fourteen muffins were sold. That number was given in the problem.
distractors.b: Dara found the muffins left by subtracting, in the next step.
distractors.d: Dara checked her answer by adding at the end, not by multiplying.

items.explanation: Dara says first she needed to find how many muffins the bakery made, so she multiplied six trays by eight muffins.

support.clue: Listen for the word 'first'. Dara says what she needed to find in her first step.
support.frame: She multiplied because she needed to find ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Sam added the stickers in two boxes because he wanted the total.' A step is explained by the goal. Listen for Dara's goal in her first step.

misconceptions.a: mixes up what the numbers mean

dropdown.template: Dara used {1} to find the total number of muffins, then used {2} to find how many were left.

items.explanation: Dara multiplied six times eight to find the total, forty-eight. Then she subtracted the fourteen muffins sold to find that thirty-four are left.

support.clue: Listen to Dara's first step and her second step. Listen for the action word she uses each time and what she wanted to find.
support.frame: First, I ______ to find the total. Next, I ______ to find how many were left.
support.model: Mentor example. 'I measured the board with a ruler to find out how long it was.' The action word and the goal go together. Listen for Dara's action word and her goal in each step.

items.stem: How did Dara check her answer?

options.text: She multiplied thirty-four by fourteen.
She added thirty-four and fourteen.
She subtracted fourteen again.
She counted the trays again.

distractors.a: Multiplying is how she found forty-eight in the first step. It is not her check.
distractors.c: Subtracting again repeats the same step. A check uses a different step.
distractors.d: Dara never counts the trays a second time.

items.explanation: Dara adds thirty-four and fourteen and gets forty-eight, the number of muffins the bakery made. This shows her subtraction is correct.

support.clue: Listen to the last sentence of Dara's talk. Notice what she does with her answer.
support.model: Mentor example. 'To check that the door was locked, Ben pulled the handle one more time.' A check is one more step that tests the first result. Listen for Dara's check.

misconceptions.c: repeats the step instead of checking it
misconceptions.d: adds a detail that was not said

items.stem: Put the events from the bridge story in order.

items.text: The children crossed first on opening day.
Heavy rain made the creek rise.
The town finished a stone bridge.

items.explanation: The rain came first, then the neighbors met, then the town finished the bridge in the fall, and the children crossed on opening day.

support.clue: Listen for time phrases: in the spring, for weeks, in the fall, on opening day. They show the order.
support.model: Mentor example. 'In May, a family planted a tree. In July, the tree grew leaves. In October, the leaves turned red.' Time words show the order of events. Put the bridge events in order the same way.

facts: The town of Marlow Creek and its bridge are invented for this practice item.

items.stem: What does the guide say about the stone bridge today?

options.text: It is the museum where the guide works.
It is a wooden crossing near the school.
It is the newest bridge in town.
It is the oldest bridge in town.

distractors.a: The guide welcomes visitors to the museum, but the bridge is a different place.
distractors.b: The wooden crossing washed away in the spring. The stone bridge replaced it.
distractors.c: The guide says the stone bridge is the oldest bridge in town, not the newest.

items.explanation: The guide ends by saying that today the stone bridge is still the oldest bridge in town.

support.clue: Listen to the last sentence of the talk. It starts with the word 'Today'.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Long ago, a baker sold bread from a cart. Today, his shop is a busy cafe.' The word today tells what is true now. Listen for what the guide says is true now.

misconceptions.a: mixes up two places in the talk
misconceptions.b: mixes up the old crossing and the new bridge

facts: The town of Marlow Creek and its bridge are invented for this practice item.
